slides.title: A fast route
slides.text: Nicotine reaches the brain shortly after it's inhaled and stimulates the reward system. This fast effect is one reason the habit forms so easily.

slides.title: Getting used to it, and withdrawal
slides.text: Over time the brain gets used to nicotine. When the nicotine level drops, restlessness and craving start; the next cigarette relieves that feeling for a while.

slides.title: Habit links
slides.text: Situations like coffee, after meals or the car get paired with smoking. These links turn into triggers that spark cravings.

slides.title: It's reversible
slides.text: When you stop smoking, the brain finds its balance again. Cravings become rarer and weaker over time.

slides.title: The first hours
slides.text: A few hours after the last cigarette, craving and restlessness can begin.

slides.title: The first three days
slides.text: Symptoms usually peak in the first days: strong cravings, irritability, trouble concentrating.

slides.title: The first weeks
slides.text: Irritability and restlessness decrease within 2–4 weeks. Increased appetite can last a little longer.

slides.title: After that
slides.text: After a few months cravings become rare, but they can still come at unexpected moments in certain settings. That's normal and it passes.

slides.title: Lighter?
slides.text: There's no evidence that cigarettes marketed as "light", "ultra" or "mild" are less harmful.

slides.title: Why?
slides.text: People who smoke them often inhale more deeply or more often without realising, so they take in a similar amount of harmful substances.

slides.title: The result
slides.text: Switching to a "lighter" cigarette doesn't replace the benefits of quitting.

slides.title: Water doesn't filter it
slides.text: The water in a hookah cools the smoke but doesn't filter out most of the harmful substances.

slides.title: Long sessions
slides.text: A hookah session lasts a long time, and a lot of smoke is inhaled during it.

slides.title: Nicotine and carbon monoxide
slides.text: Hookah smoke contains nicotine, carbon monoxide and substances linked to cancer. It can be addictive.

slides.title: Sharing is a risk
slides.text: Sharing a mouthpiece can also increase the risk of spreading infections.

slides.title: Not harmless
slides.text: E-cigarettes and heated tobacco products usually contain nicotine and are addictive. Their long-term effects are still being studied.

slides.title: Legal status in Türkiye
slides.text: In Türkiye, the commercial sale of e-cigarettes and heated tobacco products is banned.

slides.title: Not a way to quit
slides.text: This camp doesn't recommend e-cigarettes or heated tobacco as a way to quit. If you use them, they're products to quit along with the rest.

slides.title: Proven support
slides.text: For quitting, behavioural support and, when needed, a doctor's assessment are recommended. ALO 171 (Türkiye) or your local quitline can point you to the right support.

slides.title: Secondhand smoke
slides.text: Everyone in a place where people smoke breathes in the harmful substances in the smoke. There's no safe level of secondhand smoke.

slides.title: For children
slides.text: Children are affected more by secondhand smoke; respiratory infections and asthma attacks can be more frequent.

slides.title: Thirdhand smoke
slides.text: Smoke residue sticks to clothes, furniture and the inside of cars and can get back into the air over time.

slides.title: A smoke-free space
slides.text: Keeping your home and car completely smoke-free is the most effective way to protect the people you love.

slides.title: Blood vessels
slides.text: Smoking damages the inner lining of blood vessels, narrows them and makes clots form more easily.

slides.title: Heart and circulation
slides.text: These effects increase the risk of heart attack, stroke and circulation problems.

slides.title: Sexual health
slides.text: Good blood flow is important for sexual function; smoking is a known risk factor for erection problems.

slides.title: When you quit
slides.text: After quitting, circulation improves and the risk decreases over time. With ongoing problems, it's important to see a doctor.

slides.title: Skin
slides.text: Smoking reduces blood flow to the skin; skin can age early and wounds can heal more slowly.

slides.title: Teeth and gums
slides.text: Smoking can cause stained teeth, bad breath and gum disease.

slides.title: Taste and smell
slides.text: In the days after quitting, your sense of taste and smell starts to recover.

slides.title: Oxygen transport
slides.text: The carbon monoxide in cigarette smoke reduces the blood's ability to carry oxygen.

slides.title: Endurance
slides.text: That's why smokers can tire and get out of breath faster with effort.

slides.title: When you quit
slides.text: In the weeks after quitting, circulation improves and lung function increases. Many people feel the difference when climbing stairs.

slides.title: Medicines can help
slides.text: Quit-smoking medicines can increase your chances of quitting by reducing withdrawal symptoms and cravings.

slides.title: The doctor's decision
slides.text: Only a doctor can decide which medicine is right for you. This app doesn't recommend medicine names or doses.

slides.title: Free in Türkiye
slides.text: In Türkiye, quit-smoking clinics give these medicines free of charge if the doctor sees fit. You can call ALO 171 for an appointment.

slides.title: Ask first
slides.text: If you're pregnant or have heart disease or a psychiatric diagnosis, talk to your doctor before trying any method.

slides.title: Why might you gain weight?
slides.text: After quitting, appetite can increase and sweet cravings can grow; there are small changes in metabolism too.

slides.title: Small steps
slides.text: Regular meals, vegetables and fruit, plenty of water and daily movement help limit sudden weight gain.

slides.title: The priority
slides.text: The health benefit of quitting smoking is far greater than the risk of a few extra kilos.

slides.title: Does smoking relax you?
slides.text: The relaxing feeling of a cigarette comes largely from relieving the withdrawal between two cigarettes.

slides.title: A vicious circle
slides.text: Withdrawal creates tension and a cigarette relieves it for a while; so smoking seems like both the cause of stress and its cure.

slides.title: After you quit
slides.text: After the withdrawal period, many people feel less tense. Breathing, movement and social support are new ways of coping.

slides.title: The first days
slides.text: After quitting you may have trouble falling or staying asleep. This is usually temporary.

slides.title: Caffeine
slides.text: Smoking speeds up how fast caffeine leaves the body. After quitting, the same amount of coffee can have a stronger effect; cut down on caffeine in the evening.

slides.title: Sleep pattern
slides.text: Going to bed at the same time every day, putting the screen away before bed and having a calm routine help.

slides.title: A ready-made opportunity
slides.text: In Ramadan, people don't smoke all day. For many, this experience shows that they can actually go hours without smoking.

slides.title: Risky hour: after iftar
slides.text: The craving can be strong right after iftar. Making an If–Then plan for that moment in advance makes it easier.

slides.title: After suhoor
slides.text: By also dropping the cigarette after suhoor, you can spread the smoke-free hours you gain from fasting across the whole day.

slides.title: Choose a quit day
slides.text: The beginning or middle of Ramadan can be a meaningful date for your quit day.

stories.title: The benefits of quitting at any age

slides.title: It's never too late
slides.text: Whatever age you quit smoking, it benefits your health.

slides.title: Quick gains
slides.text: Shortly after quitting, your heart rate and the carbon monoxide level in your blood drop.

slides.title: Long-term gains
slides.text: Over the years, the risk of heart disease, stroke and many types of cancer decreases.

slides.title: Quality of life
slides.text: Easier breathing, better taste and smell, more energy: the gains aren't only long-term.
